newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel buys $5 bln in '97 to dampen shekel.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel buys $5 bln in '97 to dampen shekel.

text.p: The (central) Bank of Israel said on Wednesday it had bought $5 billion this year to prevent the shekel from appreciating above a trading band designed to limit currency fluctuations.
Large capital inflows forced the central bank to intervene heavily in the foreign currency market, it said in a report.

The shekel is allowed to move in a trading band with parameters seven percent above or below a sliding mid-point, designed to allow for a depreciation at a rate of six percent a year against a basket of key foreign currencies.

The report pointed to a number of economic reversals in the six months to March, including a slowdown in growth, a drop in industrial output, a renewed widening of the trade gap, higher unemployment and a deviation from the budget deficit target.
Treasury officials reported earlier this month a 1.2 billion shekel budget deficit for the first quarter of 1997, adding that revenues were smaller than planned.

The central bank said: "Considering the fact that in the first quarter in all of the years preceding 1996 there was generally a relatively small deficit and even a surplus, it can be said that the budget figures this year do not guarantee that the budget deficit target will be met for the entire year."
The government has set a deficit target of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
The Bank noted a levelling off in inflation in the period under review, with the consumer price index rising an annual 9.75 percent.
It said there was no clear trend in consumption. While demand for consumer products dropped, retail trade and bank credit increased.
The unemployment rate rose in the fourth quarter of 1997 to seven percent, exceeding the rate experienced in the preceding year and a half, it said.
